cards.q: Which comment syntax spans several lines?
cards.a:
`--[[` up to `]]`

A long comment runs from `--[[` to `]]`. Two dashes alone comment only to the end of the line, and `/* */` is C, not Lua.
cards.lessonTitle: What Lua Is and Running Code

cards.q: A program has a syntax error on line 30. Does lines 1 to 29 run first?
cards.a:
No: Lua reads the whole file first, so a syntax error means nothing runs

Lua compiles the whole chunk before running any of it. A run-time error is different: it stops the program partway, after the earlier lines have run.
cards.lessonTitle: What Lua Is and Running Code

cards.q: What does `print("a", "b")` print?
cards.a:
a and b separated by a tab

print separates its values with a tab character.
cards.lessonTitle: What Lua Is and Running Code

cards.q: What does `type(type(5))` give?
cards.a:
`"string"`

`type(5)` is the string `"number"`, and the type of any string is `"string"`.

cards.q: Why write local?
cards.a:
Without it the variable is a global, shared with all the code

A variable assigned without `local` is a global that every file and library can see and overwrite, and globals are slower. Locals are visible only in their block.

cards.q: After `local a, b = 5`, what is b?
cards.a:
nil

There is no second value on the right, so b gets nil.

cards.q: What does `print(missing_variable)` do?
cards.a:
prints nil

A name that was never assigned holds nil. Reading it is fine; calling it or doing maths with it is the error.

cards.q: What are `10 / 2` and `10 // 2`?
cards.a:
`5.0` and `5`

`/` always gives a float, even when the division is exact. `//` is floor division, and with two integers it gives an integer.

cards.q: How do you test whether n is even?
cards.a:
`n % 2 == 0`

The remainder after dividing by 2 is 0 for even numbers. This works for negative numbers too, because `%` takes the sign of the divisor; `n % 2 == 1` tests for odd.

cards.q: What does `print(-7 // 2)` print?
cards.a:
-4

// rounds down (towards minus infinity), and two integers give an integer.

cards.q: What does `tonumber("abc")` return?
cards.a:
nil

tonumber returns nil when the text is not a number, so you can check it.

cards.q: What is `#"hello" .. "!"`?
cards.a:
`"5!"`

`#` binds tighter than `..`, so it is `5 .. "!"`, and `..` turns the number into text. The length of the whole joined string would need brackets: `#("hello" .. "!")`.

cards.q: Which writes no newline: print or io.write?
cards.a:
io.write: it writes exactly its arguments

`io.write` writes exactly what you give it, so add `"\n"` yourself. `print` adds tabs between arguments and a newline at the end.

cards.q: What does `io.read("n")` give when the user types `abc`?
cards.a:
nil

"n" reads a number; when the text is not one, the result is nil.

cards.q: What does `print("a" .. 1 + 2)` print?
cards.a:
a3

+ binds tighter than .., so this is "a" .. 3.

cards.q: What is Lua's "not equal" operator?
cards.a:
`~=`

Lua writes "not equal" as `~=`. The `!=` of many other languages is a syntax error in Lua.

cards.q: Does `if 0 then` run its body?
cards.a:
Yes: only false and nil count as false, and 0 is true

In Lua every value except `false` and `nil` is true, including 0 and the empty string.

cards.q: What does `print(nil or false)` print?
cards.a:
false

nil is false, so or returns its second operand, which is false.

cards.q: What does `print(4 and 5)` print?
cards.a:
5

4 is true, so and returns its second operand.

cards.q: How many times does `for i = 1, 10, 2` run?
cards.a:
Five

i takes 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. The next value, 11, is past 10, so the loop stops.

cards.q: What is the difference between while and repeat?
cards.a:
while tests before each round; repeat tests after, runs at least once, and stops when its condition becomes true

`repeat ... until cond` checks after the body and ends when `cond` is true. `while cond do` checks first and runs while `cond` is true.

cards.q: What is printed? `for i = 3, 1 do print(i) end`
cards.a:
nothing

The step is +1 and 3 is already past 1, so the loop runs zero times. Write 3, 1, -1 to count down.

cards.q: What does Lua use instead of continue?
cards.a:
`goto continue`, with a `::continue::` label

Lua has goto and labels; a `::continue::` label at the end of the loop body is the usual idiom.

cards.q: How do you read the last item of a list t?
cards.a:
`t[#t]`

Lua lists start at 1, so the last item is at index `#t`. Negative indexes do not count from the end: `t[-1]` is just the key -1, usually nil.

cards.q: Why is `t[2] = nil` a bad way to remove the second item?
cards.a:
It leaves a hole, so # and ipairs become unreliable

Setting an item to nil does not shift the others down, so `#` and `ipairs` no longer see the items after it reliably. `table.remove(t, 2)` closes the gap.

cards.q: What does this print? `local t = {5, 6, 7}  print(t[0], t[3])`
cards.a:
nil 7

Lists start at 1, so t[0] is nil and t[3] is the last item.

cards.q: What does `table.remove(t)` return?
cards.a:
the item it removed (the last one)

table.remove returns the value it took out.

cards.q: How do you remove a key from a table?
cards.a:
Assign nil to it: `t.key = nil`

A key whose value is nil does not exist. `table.remove` works on list positions, not on named keys.

cards.q: What is the difference between t.name and t[name]?
cards.a:
`t.name` is the key "name"; `t[name]` uses the value of the variable name as the key

`t.name` is short for `t["name"]`. In `t[name]`, `name` is a variable, so the key is whatever it holds.

cards.q: `local t = { x = 1, y = 2 }` What is `#t`?
cards.a:
0

# measures the list part (keys 1, 2, 3...). This table has no list part.

cards.q: Which loop visits keys in a guaranteed order?
cards.a:
ipairs over a list

ipairs goes 1, 2, 3... in order. pairs has no defined order.

cards.q: What does table.sort return?
cards.a:
Nothing: it sorts the table you gave it, in place

`table.sort(t)` changes t itself and returns nothing, so `t = table.sort(t)` would set t to nil.

cards.q: How do you sort a list of numbers from largest to smallest?
cards.a:
`table.sort(t, function(a, b) return a > b end)`

The comparison function returns true when a should come before b. `a < b` is the default ascending order.

cards.q: What does `table.concat({1, 2, 3})` give?
cards.a:
"123"

The separator defaults to an empty string.

cards.q: Why must a sort comparison use < rather than <=?
cards.a:
With `<=`, equal items both claim to come first

The function must say "a strictly before b". `<=` gives an inconsistent order, which can make `table.sort` fail with "invalid order function".

cards.q: After `local b = a`, where a is a table, does changing b[1] change a?
cards.a:
Yes: b and a are the same table

Assigning a table copies the reference, not the contents, so both names reach one table; nothing was copied.

cards.q: What does a shallow copy not copy?
cards.a:
The tables nested inside it

A shallow copy makes a new outer table with the same values. A value that is a table is the same inner table in both, so changing it shows in both.

cards.q: `local t = {}; t.self = t` What is `t.self.self == t`?
cards.a:
true

t.self is t itself, so any number of .self steps still leads to t.

cards.q: What happens when you call a two-parameter function with one argument?
cards.a:
The second parameter is nil

Lua never checks the number of arguments: missing ones are nil and extra ones are dropped.

cards.q: How do you keep only the first result of a call that returns several?
cards.a:
Put the call in brackets, `(f())`

Brackets around a call cut it to one value. A call that is not the last item in a list is also cut to one. `select(1, ...)` returns everything from the first value on.

cards.q: `local function f() return 1, 2, 3 end` What is `#{ f(), f() }`?
cards.a:
4

The first call is not last, so it gives one value; the last call gives all three: {1, 1, 2, 3}.

cards.q: What does a function without return give back?
cards.a:
No values: nil if you use the result

Using the result of a call that returned nothing gives nil.

cards.q: Why is `flag = flag or true` a bug?
cards.a:
If the caller passes false, `false or true` is true, so false can never get through

`or` replaces any false value, not only nil. Test `if flag == nil then flag = true end` to replace only a missing argument.

cards.q: How many arguments did a function receive, counting nils?
cards.a:
`select("#", ...)`

`select("#", ...)` counts every argument, including nils. `#{...}` can be wrong when there are nils, because they make holes in the table.

cards.q: What does `select(2, "a", "b", "c")` return?
cards.a:
"b", "c"

select(n, ...) returns argument n and all the ones after it.

cards.q: `local function f(...) return #{...} end` What can go wrong with f(1, nil, 3)?
cards.a:
The nil makes a hole, so the length is unreliable

A table with a nil in the middle has a hole, and `#` may report either end of it. Use `select("#", ...)`.

cards.q: What is a closure?
cards.a:
A function plus the outer local variables it uses

A closure keeps the outer locals it uses alive, even after the function that created them has returned. An anonymous function is only a closure when it captures something.

cards.q: Two counters from make_counter: do they share a count?
cards.a:
No: each call of make_counter creates a new count variable

Every call runs `local count = 0` again, so each returned function captures its own variable.

cards.q: What does this print? `local x = 1; local f = function() return x end; x = 2; print(f())`
cards.a:
2

The function shares the variable x itself, and x is 2 when f is called.

cards.q: Why does a recursive local function need `local function name`?
cards.a:
So the name exists before the body is compiled

`local f = function() ... f() ... end` compiles the body before `f` exists, so the inner `f` refers to a global, usually nil. `local function f` declares the name first.

cards.q: Is `return 1 + f(n - 1)` a tail call?
cards.a:
No: the addition still runs after f returns

A tail call is `return f(...)` with nothing left to do afterwards. Here `1 +` still has to run, so the current call must be kept.

cards.q: What does memoisation store?
cards.a:
Results already computed, looked up by input

A memo table maps inputs to results that were already worked out, so they are looked up instead of recomputed.

cards.q: Where do global variables live?
cards.a:
In the table _G: `x = 5` is the same as `_G.x = 5`

Globals are fields of the table `_G`, so you can read, set and loop over them like any table.

cards.q: What does `<const>` do?
cards.a:
Makes it a compile-time error to assign to that local after its declaration

`local x <const> = 5` stops assignments to x. If x holds a table, the table's contents can still change.

cards.q: A function says `count = count + 1` without ever declaring count. What is count?
cards.a:
A global, nil until set, so the first call fails

Undeclared names are globals. Reading the unset global gives nil, and `nil + 1` is an "arithmetic on a nil value" error.

cards.q: What does ("hello"):sub(-3) give?
cards.a:
"llo"

A negative index counts from the end, so -3 is the third character from the end, and `sub` runs to the end by default.

cards.q: Why pass true as the fourth argument of find?
cards.a:
To search for plain text instead of a pattern

Without it, the search text is a pattern and characters like `.` or `-` have special meanings. The third argument is the start position, so pass it too: `s:find(".", 1, true)`.

cards.q: What is `("abcdef"):sub(2, 4)`?
cards.a:
"bcd"

Positions 2 to 4, both included.

cards.q: What does `("a.b"):find(".")` return?
cards.a:
1 1

Without plain = true, "." is a pattern meaning any character, so it matches the first one.

cards.q: How do you match a literal dot?
cards.a:
`%.`

In Lua patterns `%` escapes a special character; a bare `.` matches any character. `[.]` also works, but `%.` is the usual way, and the backslash of other regex languages does nothing here.

cards.q: What is the difference between `.*` and `.-`?
cards.a:
`.*` takes as much as possible, `.-` as little as possible

Both repeat any character zero or more times. `.*` is greedy, `.-` is lazy.

cards.q: Which pattern checks that the WHOLE string is digits?
cards.a:
"^%d+$"

^ and $ anchor the match to the start and end, so nothing else can be around the digits.

cards.q: What does `("a1b22c333"):match("%a(%d+)")` give?
cards.a:
"1"

The first place the pattern matches is "a1", and the capture is the digits: the string "1".

cards.q: What two values does gsub return?
cards.a:
The new string and the number of replacements

`s:gsub(...)` returns the changed string and how many replacements it made. Wrap it in brackets to keep only the string.

cards.q: In a gsub replacement string, what is %1?
cards.a:
The first capture of the match

`%1` is whatever the first pair of brackets in the pattern captured. `%0` is the whole match.

"a+b+c"

- is a special character only after something it can repeat; here it is the only thing in the pattern and matches a minus. (Writing %- is clearer.)

cards.q: What does gsub do when the replacement function returns nil?
cards.a:
keeps the original match

nil or false from the function means "leave this match as it is".

cards.q: How do you show 3.14159 as 3.14?
cards.a:
`string.format("%.2f", 3.14159)`

`.2` after `%` sets the number of digits after the point. A number without a dot, as in `%2f`, sets the minimum width instead.

cards.q: Which flag aligns a value to the left of its width?
cards.a:
`-`, as in `%-10s`

`-` pads on the right so the value starts at the left. `+` shows a sign on numbers and `0` pads numbers with zeros.

cards.q: What is `string.format("%03d", 7)`?
cards.a:
"007"

Width 3, padded with zeros.

cards.q: Why collect pieces in a table and use table.concat?
cards.a:
Each `..` in a loop copies the whole growing string

Strings never change, so every `..` builds a new one. One `table.concat` at the end builds the result once.

cards.q: Why is #"é" 2?
cards.a:
# counts bytes, and é takes two bytes in UTF-8

Lua strings are bytes. Letters outside ASCII take two to four bytes in UTF-8, and # counts those bytes.

cards.q: How do you count the characters of a UTF-8 string?
cards.a:
`utf8.len(s)`

`#s` and `s:len()` both count bytes. `utf8.len` counts code points, and returns nil when the string is not valid UTF-8.

cards.q: Which operations are safe on UTF-8 text treated as bytes?
cards.a:
joining strings and searching for ASCII text

Joining and ASCII searches never split a character. Cutting, reversing and counting by byte can.

cards.q: What does setmetatable return?
cards.a:
The table you gave it, now with its metatable set

`setmetatable(t, mt)` returns t, which is why `local obj = setmetatable({}, mt)` works in one line.

cards.q: Which metamethod does print use?
cards.a:
`__tostring`

`print` calls `tostring` on each argument, and `tostring` uses the `__tostring` metamethod when there is one. There is no `__print`.

cards.q: Two tables a and b have no metatables. What is `a + b`?
cards.a:
An error: arithmetic on a table value

Without an `__add` metamethod there is no way to add tables, so Lua raises "attempt to perform arithmetic on a table value".

cards.q: Which metamethod lets table.sort sort your objects with no comparison function?
cards.a:
__lt

table.sort compares with <, which uses __lt.

cards.q: When is __newindex called?
cards.a:
When assigning to a key the table does not have yet

Assigning to a key that already exists just changes it, with no metamethod. Reading a missing key is what `__index` handles.

cards.q: What are rawget and rawset for?
cards.a:
Reading and writing a table without its metamethods

Inside `__newindex`, a plain `t[k] = v` would call `__newindex` again forever. `rawset(t, k, v)` stores the value directly.

cards.q: `local t = setmetatable({}, { __index = { a = 1 } })` then `t.a = 2`. What is the __index table's a now?
cards.a:
1

The assignment creates a in t itself. The table behind __index is only read from.

cards.q: What does `function Account:deposit(n)` mean?
cards.a:
`function Account.deposit(self, n)`: the colon adds a first parameter called self

The colon adds a hidden first parameter, `self`. Calling `acc:deposit(10)` passes `acc` as that first argument.

cards.q: Why does `Account.__index = Account` make methods work?
cards.a:
Missing keys on an object are looked up in Account

The objects have no method fields of their own. When `acc.deposit` is missing, Lua follows the metatable's `__index` to Account and finds it there; nothing is copied.

cards.q: An object o of a class with method `function C:get() return self.v end`. What does `o.get()` do?
cards.a:
fails: self is nil, so self.v is an error

With a dot nothing is passed for self. Write o:get().

cards.q: How does a Dog method call Animal's version of the same method?
cards.a:
`Animal.method(self, ...)`

Call the base class's function with a dot and pass `self` yourself. `self:method()` would find Dog's own method again, and Lua has no `super`.

cards.q: What makes Dog fall back to Animal?
cards.a:
`setmetatable(Dog, { __index = Animal })`

Lookups on Dog that fail go through Dog's metatable, so that metatable's `__index` must be Animal. `Dog.__index` is what Dog's own objects use to reach Dog.

cards.q: rex is a Dog; Dog inherits from Animal. Where is `rex.sound` found if only Animal.new set it?
cards.a:
In rex itself

Animal.new stored `sound` in the table that became rex. Data fields live in the object; only methods are found through the class chain.

cards.q: What should the last line of a module file be?
cards.a:
`return M`

`require` gives back whatever the module file returns, so the file ends by returning the table holding its public functions.

cards.q: What happens the second time a program requires the same module?
cards.a:
Nothing is loaded again: require returns the same table, stored in package.loaded

`require` caches each module's result in `package.loaded`, so every caller shares one module table.

cards.q: Inside a module, how do you keep a helper function private?
cards.a:
make it local and do not put it in the returned table

Only what is in the returned table is visible to other files. Locals stay inside the module.

cards.q: Which file does require("ui.button") load from the current folder?
cards.a:
ui/button.lua

Dots in a module name become folder separators.

cards.q: What does error(msg, 2) change?
cards.a:
The position in the message: level 2 points at the caller, not the error line itself

The level picks which function's position is added to the message. Level 2 blames the caller, which is right when the caller passed a bad argument.

cards.q: What does pcall return when the function fails?
cards.a:
`false` and the error value

`pcall` catches the error and returns false followed by the error. On success it returns true followed by the function's results.

cards.q: What does `pcall(error, "x")` return?
cards.a:
false, "x"

pcall catches the error and returns false and the error value. error called from pcall has no Lua line to add.

cards.q: Why use xpcall instead of pcall?
cards.a:
Its handler runs before the stack unwinds

`pcall` returns after the stack is gone; `xpcall`'s handler still sees where the error happened, so it can record a traceback.

cards.q: When does a generic for loop stop?
cards.a:
When the iterator returns nil as its first value

The generic for calls the iterator each round and stops as soon as its first result is nil.

cards.q: How do you check whether a table is empty?
cards.a:
`next(t) == nil`

`#` only measures the list part, so a table with only named keys has length 0. `t == {}` compares two different tables and is always false.

cards.q: What does an iterator made with a closure keep between calls?
cards.a:
its position, in an upvalue

The closure's local variables remember where it got to.

cards.q: What does coroutine.yield(x) do?
cards.a:
Pauses the coroutine and makes the resume that ran it return true and x

A yielded coroutine can be resumed later and continues right after the yield. Returning from its function is what ends it.

cards.q: What is the difference between create and wrap?
cards.a:
create needs resume; wrap gives a function that resumes it

`coroutine.resume` returns a success flag first. The function from `wrap` returns just the yielded values and raises any error instead.

cards.q: A coroutine yields 3 times and then returns. How many resumes run it to the end?
cards.a:
4

Each resume runs up to the next yield; the fourth runs from the last yield to the end.

cards.q: What does io.open("x.txt", "w") do to an existing x.txt?
cards.a:
Empties it

Mode "w" truncates an existing file to nothing. Use "a" to append to the end instead.

cards.q: What does `local f <close> = ...` guarantee?
cards.a:
f is closed when the block ends, normally or with an error

A `<close>` variable's `__close` metamethod runs when the variable goes out of scope, so the file is closed at a known moment.

cards.q: What does io.open return for a file that does not exist (mode "r")?
cards.a:
nil and an error message

io.open reports expected failures with nil and a message; wrap it in assert to turn that into an error.

cards.q: How does a C function return two values to Lua?
cards.a:
It pushes both onto the stack and returns 2

A C function returns the number of results it left on top of the Lua stack.

cards.q: What does a host leave out to stop scripts from touching files?
cards.a:
The io and os libraries

Instead of `luaL_openlibs`, which opens every library, the host opens only the ones it wants. Without io and os, scripts cannot reach files or run commands.

cards.q: Which feature from this course does LuaJIT not have?
cards.a:
the integer subtype and //

LuaJIT follows Lua 5.1, where every number is a float; integers and // came in 5.3.

cards.q: What does a free name like `width` mean inside a chunk?
cards.a:
`_ENV.width`: a field of the chunk's environment

Free names are looked up in `_ENV`. That is `_G` unless the chunk was loaded with another environment.

cards.q: Why pass `"t"` as the mode to `load`?
cards.a:
It refuses precompiled bytecode

Mode `"t"` accepts only source text. Lua does not check bytecode, which can be crafted to crash or attack the interpreter.

cards.q: A script is loaded with load(code, "s", "t", {}). What happens if it calls print("hi")?
cards.a:
An error: print is nil there

The environment is an empty table, so `print` is not in it; the sandbox hands over only what you put in it.

cards.q: Why does an ordinary table used as a cache leak memory?
cards.a:
Its references keep every cached object alive

None of the objects can become unreachable, so none is collected. A weak table (`__mode = "k"` or `"v"`) does not count as a reference.
cards.lessonTitle: Weak Tables and the Garbage Collector

cards.q: When should a resource be released with `__close` rather than `__gc`?
cards.a:
When it must be released at a known moment

`__close` runs as soon as the variable goes out of scope. `__gc` runs whenever the collector gets to the object, which may be much later.
cards.lessonTitle: Weak Tables and the Garbage Collector

cards.q: A table has __mode = "k". When does an entry with a table as its key disappear?
cards.a:
when that key table is not reachable from anywhere else

Weak keys do not keep their objects alive; once nothing else refers to the key, the entry can be removed.
cards.lessonTitle: Weak Tables and the Garbage Collector

cards.q: What is `-7 // 2` in Lua?
cards.a:
`-4`

Floor division rounds down, towards negative infinity, so -3.5 becomes -4. Rounding towards zero (-3) is what C does.
cards.lessonTitle: Integers, Bitwise Operators and Binary Data

cards.q: What is the difference between `a ~ b` and `~a`?
cards.a:
`a ~ b` is bitwise XOR; `~a` is bitwise NOT

With two operands `~` is exclusive OR; with one it flips every bit. "Not equal" is `~=`.
cards.lessonTitle: Integers, Bitwise Operators and Binary Data

cards.q: What does string.unpack("<I2", "\x01\x02") return first?
cards.a:
513

Little-endian puts the low byte first: 0x01 + 0x02 * 256 = 513.
cards.lessonTitle: Integers, Bitwise Operators and Binary Data

cards.q: Why is `table.remove(t, 1)` slow for a big queue?
cards.a:
It moves every remaining element down one place

Removing at position 1 shifts all other items. A queue with first and last indexes moves nothing.

cards.q: In a heap stored in a list, where are the children of position 5?
cards.a:
At positions 10 and 11

In a list starting at 1, the children of position i are at 2i and 2i + 1. Positions 9 and 10 would be the rule for a heap starting at 0.

cards.q: How is membership tested quickly in Lua?
cards.a:
by storing the members as keys and checking set[x]

Keys are looked up directly, in constant time.

cards.q: Why write `(s:gsub(...))` with brackets inside a pipeline?
cards.a:
gsub returns two values, and the brackets keep only the first

`gsub` returns the new string and the number of replacements. Without the brackets the next function would receive the count as an extra argument.

cards.q: Why use `table.pack(...)` instead of `{...}` in `partial`?
cards.a:
It records the number of values in `n`, so nil arguments are kept in place

With `{...}`, a nil argument makes a hole and `#` can be wrong. `table.pack` stores the real count in field `n`.

cards.q: F.reduce({1, 2, 3}, function(a, b) return a * b end, 1) gives...
cards.a:
6

It multiplies 1 by each element in turn: 1 * 1 * 2 * 3.

cards.q: Why sort the keys when saving?
cards.a:
So the same data always gives the same text

`pairs` visits keys in no fixed order. Without sorting, saving the same data twice can give different files, which makes changes hard to compare.

cards.q: What stops loaded data from calling `os.exit`?
cards.a:
Loading it with an empty environment table

With an empty `_ENV`, names like `os` and `io` do not exist inside the chunk. `pcall` only catches errors; it would not stop `os.exit`.

cards.q: What does string.format("%q", 'a "b"\n') produce?
cards.a:
Lua source that reads back as the same string

`%q` writes a string as a quoted Lua literal, with the quotes and the new line escaped, so loading it gives the same string.

cards.q: Why are closure-object methods called with a dot instead of a colon?
cards.a:
They take no self; their data is in captured variables

Each method already reaches its object's data through captured locals, so it needs no `self` argument.

cards.q: What does `__call` on a class's metatable allow?
cards.a:
Calling the class like a function: `Point(1, 2)`

When a table with a `__call` metamethod is called, Lua runs that function with the table and the arguments, which makes a neat constructor.

cards.q: Which pattern keeps fields private so no outside code can read them?
cards.a:
closures that capture local variables

Local variables captured by closures cannot be reached from outside at all.

cards.q: Why is `s = s .. piece` in a long loop slow?
cards.a:
Each step copies the whole string built so far

Strings never change, so each `..` builds a new string and the work grows with the square of the pieces. Collect them in a table and join once with `table.concat`.

cards.q: What should you do before optimising a piece of code?
cards.a:
Measure it, to see whether and where it is slow

Guesses about speed are often wrong. Measuring shows whether the code matters and which part to work on.

cards.q: Which is usually fastest for joining 10,000 numbers with commas?
cards.a:
`table.concat(t, ",")` on a table of them

`table.concat` builds the result once instead of copying a growing string again and again.
